Topic: If a nation's merchants and manufacturers persuade its legislators to grant them a monopoly of the home market, by what reckoning can the consumer, whose interest alone is the sole end of all production, be said to gain anything other than dearer goods and a smaller share of the annual produce of the land and labour of the country?
Machiavelli — Judgement:
You ask a merchant's question, but it is really a question of who rules. When manufacturers buy the legislator's pen, the issue is not the price of cloth. The issue is which humour of the city has captured the state.

In every city there are two humours: the great, who wish to command and oppress, and the people, who wish only not to be oppressed. A monopoly is the great oppressing by statute rather than by sword, and your "consumer" is simply the people called by a new name. I have written that a prince can never make himself secure against a hostile people, because they are too many. Yet the legislator who lets a faction of the rich tax the many through the market turns those many into his enemies, and he gets only a few greedy friends in return.

The consumer gains nothing but dearer bread, and the state loses more, because the legislator who sells the home market sells the people's loyalty with it.

*Whoever lets the few grow fat on the many has traded away the only wall that defends a state.*
Keynes — Judgement:
Adam Smith's reckoning is sound only when every man who wants work already has it. I came to distrust that assumption, because the slump of the 1930s showed that idle men and idle mills can last for years.

In *The General Theory* I gave the old mercantilists their due. When effective demand is deficient, the consumer is also the unemployed labourer, and goods kept at home may set wasted resources to work. That can enlarge the annual produce rather than shrink it. But a monopoly that merchants obtain by lobbying is not a policy for employment. It is a private toll on the public, and it protects interests that do better from scarcity than from output. The real question is whether the State will raise demand directly, through public works and cheap money, so that no industry needs to beg for shelter.

A merchants' monopoly of the home market robs the consumer. It only seems otherwise when demand is deficient, and the State should cure that by spending, not by granting privilege.

*Free trade is a creed for full employment, and in a slump the remedy is demand, never a merchant's monopoly.*
Hayek — Judgement:
Smith asked the right question, and I would sharpen it: a protected home market is not merely a transfer from consumer to producer but the deliberate silencing of the price system, that telecommunications network through which dispersed individuals learn what none could otherwise know.

When legislators grant such a privilege, they do not simply raise prices; they abolish competition as a discovery procedure, so that no one ever learns which goods might have been made more cheaply, by whom, or where. Consumers lose not only what they pay but what would have been found. And, as I argued in Law, Legislation and Liberty, an unlimited legislature becomes the plaything of organised interests, buying the votes of concentrated groups at the expense of the dispersed many who cannot combine.

By no reckoning whatever does the consumer gain: such a monopoly is a privilege extracted by political bargaining, and it impoverishes the whole society by suppressing knowledge that only competition can reveal.

*Protection does not shelter an industry; it blindfolds a nation.*
